title: ME05a: Simple Rules for the Self and the Role
author: Richard Claydon
summary: Claydon uses a fictional leader, Maya, to introduce the first two of five simple rules for leading in complexity. Rule one is to develop the self who can evolve the role, drawing on McAdams's three layers of traits, characteristic adaptations and narrative identity rather than personality-type shorthand. Maya replaces psychometric labels with a narrative Talent Profile, and her team's honest responses show who is open to growth and who, like the brittle Kieran, is not. Rule two is to work on one thing to improve all things, illustrated by her own 360 feedback, where changing one behaviour shifted several derailers. The narrative device makes the ideas concrete but keeps the argument light, and it closes with reflection prompts.
points: Type labels such as colour wheels and strengths inventories rarely hold under pressure; how a self adapts in role and narrates its work matters more.
A prompt-based Talent Profile that asks about role, struggles and hopes surfaces development needs that performance reviews miss.
Leaders can refuse to engage in narrative development, and that refusal is itself a risk in systems moving toward emergence.
Choosing one behaviour to change, such as listening without defensiveness, can ripple across several related derailers.
Development in complex systems comes from one coherent move that unlocks others, not from overhauling everything.
quotes: What she needed now wasn’t more clarity for herself. It was grammar for the collective. Something her team could hold on to when certainty failed.
Most of us have been through the psychometric parade—MBTI, DiSC, colour wheels, strengths inventories. They can be useful, in parts. But under pressure, they rarely hold.
What mattered more wasn’t type. It was how a self showed up in-role, under strain, entangled int he system, and whether that self could evolve.

Traits matter, but they’re entry-level—useful for strangers, not for leadership. Adaptations and narratives are where the real work happens: how we adjust, how we integrate, how we make sense of ourselves in motion.
These weren’t performance reviews. They were narratives. Invitations to be seen in-role, not just judged in function.
Six months later, something remarkable happened: not only had her openness scores improved, but her Need to Control and Hostility had dropped—without ever targeting them directly.
That insight stuck: in complex systems, development isn’t about overhauling everything. It’s about one coherent move that unlocks others.
